lesson.menu_desc: Reading model -- the redline round: redline, boilerplate, sticking point, cap, carve-out, side letter, walk away, good faith, fallback, subject to contract -- and "would" for hypothetical offers and softened proposals -- 29 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 22 -- Contract Negotiation -- The Redline Round
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Simone Quiles de Santana Marques | Lesson 22 -- Contract Negotiation
lesson.grammar_point: would for hypothetical offers and softened proposals (we would be prepared to / would you be willing to)

listenings.text: Simone, the draft came back from the other side last night and I want you to know what you are walking into before Wednesday. There are forty redlines in the document, and thirty-five of them are boilerplate. Do not spend one minute on those. Five of them matter. The real sticking point is the liability cap. They want it at one times the annual fee, and our client cannot live with that. Here is how I would like you to handle it. Do not say no. Say we would be prepared to move on the cap if they accepted a carve-out for fraud, and see what comes back. If they refuse everything, our fallback is a side letter that covers the same ground without touching the main document, but do not put that on the table on Wednesday. And please remember to write subject to contract at the top of every email you send them this week. Nothing you write is binding until the contract is signed, and I want that in black and white. If the tone turns hard, stay in good faith and keep the door open. Nobody is going to walk away over a carve-out.

It is Tuesday night and I am building the script for tomorrow. Forty redlines, and I have already put thirty-five of them in the boilerplate pile. I accept those without a word, because arguing about a standard clause is how a round dies of old age. The five that are left go on one page, and at the top of that page, in capital letters, is the sticking point: the liability cap. My rule for tomorrow is that I never open my mouth with the word no. Every answer starts with would. We would be prepared to move on the cap if you accepted a carve-out for fraud. Would you be willing to look at a longer notice period instead? It costs me nothing, it concedes nothing, and it tells them exactly what trade I am looking for. If they close the door on all five, I have a fallback in my folder, a short side letter that covers the same ground outside the main document, and I am not showing it tomorrow. Every email goes out marked subject to contract, so nothing I write this week binds my client. And whatever the tone becomes at eleven o'clock, I stay in good faith, because nobody should have to walk away from a good deal over one carve-out.

extra_audio.text: First, the draft comes back from the other side and you read every redline in the document. Then, you separate the boilerplate, which you accept without arguing, from the five changes that really matter to your client. After that, you name the sticking point out loud, because a round that never names it goes in circles for weeks. Next, you make a softened offer instead of a refusal: we would be prepared to move on the cap if you accepted a carve-out for fraud. Finally, if the other side refuses everything, you take out your fallback, you keep the conversation in good faith, and you never walk away in the same meeting.

reading.rtitle: Why Nobody Says No in a Contract Round
paras: A contract negotiation looks like an argument about words, and it almost never is. The draft comes back with forty changes marked in the text, and the first job of the lawyer who receives it is not to answer them. It is to sort them. Most of those redlines are boilerplate: the standard clauses that appear in every contract of that kind, where the other side has simply pasted its own house version. Fighting them costs days and wins nothing.

Under the boilerplate there are usually four or five changes that decide the deal, and one of them is the sticking point. It is often the liability cap, because that is where the money actually sits. Everyone in the room knows which one it is. What separates a round that closes from a round that runs for two months is whether somebody names it out loud on the first call.

Then comes the part that surprises people who do not do this for a living: almost nobody says no. A flat refusal ends the exchange and tells the other side nothing about what you could accept. So the answer comes back softened, and hypothetical: we would be prepared to move on the cap if you accepted a carve-out for fraud. Nothing has been conceded, the door is open, and the other side now knows the shape of the trade.

Behind that sentence there is always a fallback that nobody mentions yet, and quite often it is a side letter that covers the same ground outside the main document. And above all of it, at the top of every email, sit three words that keep the week safe: subject to contract. They mean that nothing written so far binds anybody. That is what allows both sides to argue in good faith for a fortnight and still be able to walk away without owing each other a thing.

reading.prompt: Read once, quickly. Which title fits the whole text best?
choices: How to write the standard clauses of a commercial contract
A contract round is about sorting the changes, naming the one that matters, and answering with a softened, hypothetical offer instead of a refusal
Why liability caps should always be set at one times the annual fee

items: The text says the first job is to answer every redline in the draft.
The first job is to SORT them, not to answer them: most are boilerplate and fighting them wins nothing.
Naming the sticking point out loud early is what separates a fast round from a slow one.
Everyone knows which change it is; the round that closes is the one where somebody names it on the first call.
According to the text, a flat refusal is the strongest answer you can give.
The opposite. A flat refusal ends the exchange and tells the other side nothing about what you could accept.
"Subject to contract" means that what you have written so far is already binding.
It means the opposite: nothing written so far binds anybody until the contract is signed.
The fallback is usually kept back and not mentioned at the start.
The text says there is always a fallback that nobody mentions yet -- often a side letter outside the main document.
